<reason>Both sides argued competently with plausible closed-book reasoning, but CON landed the more damaging rebuttals and controlled the decisive comparisons. CON's "name the judge" pressure was a genuine burden on the motion's conditional trigger, and its follow-up — that PRO's proposed proxies (time-to-match, ghosting rates) are "engagement metrics wearing a lab coat" that would encode one romantic ideal — materially damaged PRO's procedural answer. CON also defused PRO's headline "concession" by distinguishing an imperfect reciprocity proxy from a corrupted signal, a distinction PRO's closing restated past rather than answered. Most decisively, CON caught an internal inconsistency in PRO's own remedy: paid extra likes and paid filters are themselves paid visibility, so PRO renames the toll booth while removing the underserved user's only lever — a point PRO left unaddressed through the closing. PRO's best work was the Match Group ownership reply, the short-term-metrics-beat-long-term-reputation mechanism, and a genuinely strong closing reframe ("you cannot vote with your feet against a manipulation you've been engineered not to notice"), which CON answered adequately with the folk vocabulary of swipe fatigue and Tinder's user slide. PRO also underused its best structural asset — that the motion is conditional, so CON's measurability objection is practical rather than normative. Both hit the Q/A format requirements cleanly; both openings were clipped equally.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 catch that PRO's replacement revenue — paid extra likes, filters, read receipts — is itself paid visibility, so PRO's "remove the toll booth" claim collapses while the underserved 45-year-old loses his one way to be seen. PRO never answered it.</best_rebuttal>
